title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: A decade of compounding built a $447 billion revenue franchise, yet $131 billion of acquisition goodwill and a 2025 ROIC dip below WACC remind us that capital allocation discipline is as vital as underwriting.
epigraph.author: 10-Year Financial Forensics (2016–2026 YTD)

web_blocks.title: 10-Year P&L, Margin Bridge, and Cash Conversion (2016–2025 + 9M 2026)

web_blocks.html: From FY2016 through FY2025, UnitedHealth Group more than doubled its top line. Consolidated revenue grew from $184.84 billion in 2016 to $447.57 billion in 2025, a 10.3% nine-year CAGR [18], [24]. Through 2023, operating profit scaled even faster, rising from $12.93 billion (7.00% margin) to $32.36 billion (8.71% margin) [24]. That streak broke in 2024 and 2025. Revenue kept rising (+7.7% in 2024; +11.8% in 2025), yet operating profit stalled at $32.29 billion in 2024 before dropping 41.3% to $18.96 billion in 2025 (4.24% margin) [3], [18]. An 89.1% MCR, Change Healthcare costs, and a $(278) million Optum Health loss drove the drop. In 9M 2026, operating profit rebounded to $23.54 billion on $336.45 billion of revenue (7.00% margin) [19].

web_blocks.caption: 10-Year Consolidated Financial Forensics & Cash Conversion (2016–2025 + 9M 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: FCF exceeded Net Income in every single year from 2016 through 2025, demonstrating durable cash conversion even during the 2024–2025 earnings drawdown.

web_blocks.title: Balance Sheet Quality: Acquisition Goodwill, Leverage, and ROIC vs. WACC

web_blocks.html: A balance-sheet audit shows why ROIC fell faster than operating margins. Serial buyouts—DaVita Medical, Change Healthcare (~$13B), LHC Group ($5.4B), and Amedisys ($3.3B)—lifted goodwill and intangibles to roughly $131 billion by year-end 2025 [18]. Those assets equal 42% of total assets. To fund deals, buybacks, and dividends, long-term debt rose to $71,794 million against $94,110 million of equity [18]. That leaves Debt-to-Equity near 0.76x and a Current Ratio of 0.74x. FY2025 interest expense reached $4,002 million [18].

Invested capital grew from ~$241B–$252B in 2023 to ~$271B–$312B across 2025–2026 [25]. As profit fell in 2025, ROIC dropped from ~14.4%–17.0% in 2023 to ~6.1%–9.4% in FY2025 and ~6.5%–7.5% TTM in 2026 [25]. It slipped below UNH estimated WACC of ~8.6% [25]. To restore a positive spread, UNH must lift operating margins toward 6.5%–7.5% and pause debt-funded mega-deals.

web_blocks.title: Capital Allocation: Share Count Reduction and Dividend Compounding

web_blocks.html: Cash conversion (CFO / Net Income) stayed strong through the storm. It averaged over 120% for the decade and hit 163% in FY2025 ($19.70B CFO vs. $12.06B common net income) [18], [24]. Management used excess cash to cut share count from ~951.2 million in 2016 to ~902 million by Q3 2026 (~896 million basic/float) [20]. Annual dividends tripled from ~$2.63 in 2016 to $8.73 in 2025 ($2.32 quarterly in Q2/Q3 2026) [20]. Keeping that dividend safe while paying down debt requires steady margin gains.

web_blocks.title: Forensic Takeaway: Cash Conversion Held Up, Capital Efficiency Did Not
paragraphs: UnitedHealth Group never faced a cash-flow crisis in 2024–2025. Free cash flow stayed above $16 billion even at the trough.
The real flaw was capital efficiency. Carrying $131 billion of goodwill and $71.8 billion of debt pushed ROIC below WACC, making margin repair and debt paydown top priorities.

web_blocks.title: Effective Tax Rate, Noncontrolling Interests, and Leverage Discipline

web_blocks.html: Two items below operating profit also deserve note. First, the effective tax rate fell to 12.9% in FY2025 ($1,890 million tax on $14,697 million pre-tax profit), down from 19%–22% norms [18], [24]. Tax-exempt income and divestiture adjustments drove the dip. Second, noncontrolling interests totaled $751 million in FY2025 ($12,807 million total profit minus $12,056 million common profit) [18], [24]. That reflects doctor-partner stakes in Optum Health and SCA Health clinics. Pausing buyouts lets $16.1B+ in annual FCF strengthen the balance sheet organically [18], [20].

book_paragraphs: When you and I open UnitedHealth Group's ten-year financial ledger from 2016 through 2025, we see two completely different stories stitched together. The first eight years, from 2016 to 2023, read like a textbook compounding machine. Revenue more than doubled from $184.84 billion to $371.62 billion. Operating income marched upward every single year without a blemish, climbing from $12.93 billion to $32.36 billion as operating margins expanded from 7.0% to 8.71%. Free cash flow compounded from $8.10 billion to $25.71 billion, comfortably exceeding net income every year.

Then look at 2024 and 2025. Revenue didn't slow down at all—it jumped to $400.28 billion in 2024 and $447.57 billion in 2025. Yet operating earnings stalled at $32.29 billion in 2024 and collapsed 41% to $18.96 billion in 2025, cutting the operating margin in half to 4.24%. Notice the cash flow statement, though: even in the teeth of that 2025 earnings storm, operating cash flow reached $19.70 billion against $3.62 billion of capital expenditures, generating $16.08 billion of free cash flow—more than 133% of common net income.

Now look at the first nine months of 2026. Revenue sits at $336.45 billion, and operating earnings have already rebounded to $23.54 billion—a 7.00% operating margin that puts the enterprise back on track toward historical earning power.

So where is the real scar from the last five years? You find it on the balance sheet, not the cash flow statement. To build out Optum Health and Optum Insight, management spent tens of billions acquiring DaVita Medical, Change Healthcare for $13 billion, LHC Group for $5.4 billion, and Amedisys for $3.3 billion. By year-end 2025, goodwill and intangible assets swelled to $131 billion—roughly 42% of total consolidated assets—while long-term debt reached $71.79 billion against $94.11 billion of shareholders' equity, carrying a $4.0 billion annual interest tab.

That bloated invested-capital base—now roughly $271 billion to $312 billion—explains why Return on Invested Capital fell from 14%–17% in 2023 down to 6.1%–9.4% in 2025 and roughly 6.5%–7.5% on a trailing basis in 2026, slipping beneath an estimated 8.6% cost of capital. Meanwhile, management kept returning cash to owners, trimming the share count from 951 million in 2016 to roughly 902 million by Q3 2026 and raising the annual dividend from $2.63 to $8.73 per share in 2025. Going forward, you and I want to see Hemsley and DeVeydt let organic margin recovery lift ROIC back above WACC rather than adding another dollar of acquisition goodwill.

Two quieter details in the financial statements deserve your attention before we close the forensic audit. First, notice the $751 million gap in FY2025 between consolidated net earnings of $12,807 million and common shareholders' net income of $12,056 million. That gap represents physician partners who co-own Optum Health clinics and SCA Health surgery centers—a reminder that vertical care delivery shares its upside with local doctors even when the parent absorbs capitation losses.

Second, notice how resilient the dividend and buyback engine remained despite the 2025 margin trough. Because free cash flow held at $16.08 billion, UNH still funded $8.73 per share in 2025 dividends and trimmed the share count toward 902 million by Q3 2026. Now, with $71.79 billion of long-term debt costing $4.0 billion a year in interest and ROIC sitting below an 8.6% cost of capital, the smartest capital-allocation move for 2027 is simple: let organic earnings recovery rebuild the ROIC-versus-WACC spread while keeping the M&A checkbook closed.

book_callouts.label: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.title: Goodwill Is the Silent Denominator
book_callouts.text: When an acquirer puts $131 billion of goodwill and intangibles on its balance sheet, every basis point of operating-margin compression hits ROIC twice as hard. UNH's path back to a positive ROIC-minus-WACC spread runs through organic pricing discipline and debt reduction, not more M&A.
